The humble cactus is an icon of resiliency. Stuck in a desert with little rain and abundant searing sun, these plants don’t just survive, they thrive—and in turn provide habitat for owls and other birds, and flowers for bats and other pollinators.
Yet cacti are in serious trouble , due to habitat loss and the poaching of species for private collections. Now we can add worsening droughts to those woes, according to a new study in the journal Nature. Researchers modeled a future of not just relentlessly rising temperatures but also the attendant dry spells, finding that the majority of nearly 1,000 cactus species will lose habitat as the climate radically changes. More than a quarter of those species could lose at least 80 percent of that habitat by 2100.
“The public perception of cacti tends to be of these organisms that are extremely drought-adapted and are just resilient, can handle anything that you throw at them,” said Michiel Pillet, a conservation ecologist at the University of South Florida and lead author of the paper. “In reality, cacti are absolutely amazing—and they’re my favorite plant group, clearly—but they’re not that different from other plants.”
That means cacti need water. In the deserts of the southwestern United States, for example, they rely on seasonal monsoon rains, which tend to make July or August the wettest month in a given year . Because this is still a desert, cacti have evolved a range of adaptations to survive , like a waxy skin that helps them retain that bounty of rainwater. “Just like other plants, they evolved under conditions that they’re used to,” Pillet said. “When you take them outside of those conditions, they might not be able to handle that.”
Think of these cacti like sick hospital patients. Someone might be admitted for heat-related illness, as their body struggles to cool itself. At the same time, though, they might be dehydrated. Cacti are dealing with the same stresses, as global temperatures rise and dry spells intensify. “When we consider drought conditions, then it turns out that they’re much, much sicker than we previously thought,” Pillet said. “These results really do change the outlook of cacti, and most likely plants more broadly under climate change.”
Instead of simply modeling these threats going forward, the researchers turned to the citizen science platform iNaturalist, where people upload photos of plants and animals. This provided 650,000 observations of cacti in the wild, helping paint a clearer picture of how species might be faring.
Really, this isn’t a simple matter of cacti withering and dying. Sure, if relentless droughts take hold, individuals can’t get water. But the stress could be temporally complex, too. “Now we can move towards questions of: What life stages are most affected?” Pillet said. “Is it the adults or is it the seedlings? But also, which processes? Is it reduced growth or is it increased mortality? Or are plants failing to flower?”
Put another way: Cactus species could be suffering from sublethal effects of drought—the lack of water may not kill them immediately but still interfere with their reproduction. And without procreation, populations shrink. In the Sonoran Desert, for example, the iconic, towering saguaro is reproducing less frequently during prolonged droughts, because they’re not always flowering.
Part of the problem is that while desert ecosystems may look tough and hardened overall, they’re in fact quite fragile. “They don’t recover quickly once they are disturbed, or once they are degraded, just because there’s so little water and such higher temperatures,” said Marcos Robles, the Nature Conservancy’s lead scientist in Arizona, who wasn’t involved in the research. “It takes multiple decades to recover, and in some cases, they don’t recover.”
Now drought is compounding with other stressors, like habitat loss and poaching, to drive cactus species to the brink. On the opposite end of the spectrum, too much water from rising seas has led to the local extinction of the Key Largo tree cactus in Florida. Higher nighttime temperatures are a problem, too, since that’s when saguaro and other cacti respire to avoid water loss. “If the nighttime temperatures are very high, they can’t do it,” said Rod Haenni, president of the nonprofit Cactus and Succulent Society of America, who wasn’t involved in the paper. “Then if you water on top of that, the plants just rot.”
Still, some cactus species may persist by picking up and leaving. Well, not individual plants, but populations could creep into areas with climates that more closely match what the species adapted to all those millennia ago. A similar thing is happening in the Arctic, actually, where some plants are marching farther north in “search” of increasingly agreeable weather and more water.
In the end, the purpose of this sort of research is to better inform where conservation professionals might concentrate their efforts. They can’t stop droughts, of course, but they can evacuate enough cacti to establish populations in botanical gardens, where they can be cared for as the climate grows more unrecognizable to even the hardiest desert vegetation. Species can even be reintroduced to the wild in some cases, so long as drought and high temperatures don’t remain a threat to a population.
Governments, too, need to protect the lands where cacti are threatened, Haenni said. This new research, he added, could make that happen. “Hopefully, it’ll wake people up,” Haenni said. “But the problem is that a lot of the governments involved are indifferent to this. There are a lot of people in the countries who are not indifferent, but they’re not running the governments.”
This story originally appeared on Grist and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

STARBASE, Texas —The black and silver ship fell out of the sky, emerging from the cloud deck near the very end of its flight. Incongruously, the rocket flew horizontal until the last moment when three Raptor rocket engines ignited and it swooped into a vertical position.
Slowly, gently, haltingly, the Starship upper stage eased its way toward the waiting tower where two arms extended outward, awaiting expectantly. The margins are so incredibly narrow. Two nubs on either side of the rocket, each protruding only about one foot, were the only purchase the rocket would have on the arms.
Then, less than a minute after it came into view, the Starship upper stage was snagged by the launch tower, as snug as you like. And so it was all over. SpaceX, nearly a quarter of a century after its founding, had just taken a hugely significant step toward developing and optimizing a massive, rapidly reusable rocket.
This was a breathtaking feat; a brilliant technical achievement that required the best engineering minds to think through a million different, difficult problems. And on Saturday evening, following a handful of practice runs into the Indian Ocean, they did it before the entire world.
Watching Starship launch from here a little less than a day earlier, and knowing it had orbited the planet multiple times, added to the sense of unreality in seeing this spaceship return to Earth under its own power, and be captured by the tower.
It felt like stepping into the future. SpaceX has dazzled us before, by landing rockets on barges and returning humans to space with Crew Dragon. But this flight took things to another level. Starships are huge. They carry a huge amount of energy coming back from orbit. And until a few years ago, it seemed beyond fantastical to think about capturing a rocket with what are essentially outsized chopsticks.
Humans have built reusable spacecraft that flew into orbit before. In the 1970s, flush with confidence after the triumphant Moon landings, NASA designed and built several Space Shuttles. They had solid rocket boosters that were fished from the ocean and reused. The large orange external tank was not recovered after each flight, but the orbiters went to space for two weeks, or even longer, before returning to Earth and landing on a runway.
The shuttles were engineering marvels. But during the return to Earth they acted as gliders, not igniting their engines. And their heat shields were delicate flowers, requiring painstaking refurbishment after each flight. At the outset of the shuttle program, the space agency contemplated sending dozens of humans into space at a time, and carrying cargo at a cost as low of $25 per pound.
Reality never matched these rosy projections. The crew space capped out at seven astronauts, and the cost-per-pound was closer to $25,000. Each orbiter cost an extraordinary amount of money to build; NASA only ever built five that went to space.
SpaceX has five Starships in an advanced state of development at Starbase today; and its factory houses the components for a dozen more. The company can currently manufacture a Starship upper stage in its South Texas Starfactory every three weeks. The factory was sized to produce a ship every three days. When SpaceX founder Elon Musk discussed these build targets in an interview five years ago, he sounded mad. But he no longer does.
The Space Shuttle was nearly a fully reusable space launch system, but it fell far short of low-cost, rapid launch. Over 30 years the vehicle made 135 flights. Within a few years SpaceX aims to fly 135 times a year, then thousands of times.
Such was the significance of Saturday. SpaceX aspires to fundamentally change the relationship between humanity and the heavens. The first step is to get the entire rocket back. SpaceX has now returned both elements of a Starship rocket safely to its launch tower. It will take time to reach a high rate of success with such landings, but Saturday’s safe return offered a proof of concept.
The landings will come with increasing frequency; and so will the launches. Over time SpaceX will perfect the heat shield that is likely to be the most difficult aspect of rapid reuse. And eventually, as difficult as it may be to believe, what we experienced with amazement this weekend will become routine. One day, we will take this all for granted.

Bursa 'da 2012 yılında kaybolan Mehmet Şahinoğlu'nun öldürülmesine ilişkin soruşturmada gözaltına alınan 11 şüphelinin emniyetteki işlemleri tamamlandı.
Habertürk muhabiri Mustafa Şekeroğlu’nun haberine göre adliyeye sevk edilen 11 kişiden olayın baş şüphelisi Mehmet Salih A., ile eşi Saadet A., oğlu Fatih A., Faruk A. ve S.G. çıkarıldıkları mahkemece tutuklanarak cezaevine gönderildi. C.A., S.İ., R.A., M.A., F.A. ve E.G. ise adli kontrol şartıyla serbest bırakıldı.
Adalet Bakanı Akın Gürlek, faili meçhul cinayetlere ilişkin yaptığı açıklamada 76 dosyada 83 cinayetin aydınlatıldığını duyurdu. Açıklamada yer alan dosyalardan biri de Habertürk'ün mayıs ayında "Cesetler yok, dişler konuştu" başlığıyla gündeme getirdiği Mehmet Şahinoğlu cinayeti oldu. Habertürk'ün özel haberinde, yıllar önce bulunan maksilla (üst çene kemiği) parçasının Mehmet Şahinoğlu'nun diş kayıtlarıyla uyumlu çıkması ve bu delilin Yargıtay'ın beraat kararlarını bozmasındaki önemi anlatıldı.
14 yıllık cinayet dosyasında gerçekleştirilen operasyonun perde arkasında, Bursa Cinayet Büro Amirliği ekiplerinin bir yıldır gizlilik içinde yürüttüğü titiz çalışma yer aldı. Adalet Bakanlığı bünyesindeki Faili Meçhul Suçları Araştırma Daire Başkanlığının koordinasyonunda, Bursa Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığının talimatları doğrultusunda yürütülen çalışmalarda dosya yeniden mercek altına alındı.
Cinayet dedektifleri, 2015 yılında Bursa'nın Kestel ilçesinde bulunan yanmış insan kemiklerine ilişkin adli tıp raporlarını, diş kayıtlarını, iletişim verilerini ve tanık beyanlarını yeniden değerlendirdi. Elde edilen yeni bulgular üzerine 12 şüpheliye yönelik operasyon düzenlendi. Şüphelilerden 11'i yakalanırken bir kişinin firari olduğu açıklandı.
Dehşet iddialara uzanan olay 2012 yılında bir kayıp başvurusuyla başladı. Osmaniye'de TIR şoförlüğü yapan Mehmet Şahinoğlu, 2012 yılında İstanbul'a geldikten sonra esrarengiz şekilde ortadan kayboldu. İstanbul Kayıp Şahıslar Büro Amirliği ekiplerinin yürüttüğü araştırmada, Şahinoğlu'nun kısa süre önce boşandığı eşi Saime Sivri'nin de kayıp olduğu ortaya çıktı.
Soruşturma dosyasına göre Saime Sivri, daha önce Bursa'da Mehmet Salih A. ile imam nikahlı yaşıyordu. Şahinoğlu ile evlendikten sonra Mehmet Salih A.'nın girişimleriyle boşandı. İddiaya göre Mehmet Salih A., Şahinoğlu'nu İstanbul'a getirmek için bir plan hazırladı. Bu kapsamda Sultan D. isimli kadın, kendisini zengin ve dul bir kadın olarak tanıtarak Şahinoğlu ile telefon görüşmeleri yaptı. Şahinoğlu, Sultan D. ile buluşmak için 18 Ekim 2012 tarihinde İstanbul'a geldi ve bir daha kendisinden haber alınamadı.
İstanbul Kayıp Şahıslar Büro Amirliği ekiplerinin çalışmasıyla 2015 yılında aralarında Mehmet Salih A.'nın da bulunduğu şüpheliler yakalandı. Tutuklanan şüpheliler daha sonra tahliye edildi. Mehmet Salih A.'nın yeğeni Ercan Akdeniz ise 2016 yılında verdiği ifadede, amcasının talimatıyla Mehmet Şahinoğlu'nun cesedini Gemlik Kurşunlu'daki villadan çıkararak Bursa'nın Kestel ilçesinde yaktıklarını öne sürdü. Akdeniz, daha sonra mahkemede bu ifadesinden döndü. Akdeniz'in Muş'ta öldürüldüğü yönündeki bilgi üzerine Bursa Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığı, ölümün araştırılmasını ve dosyayla bağlantısının incelenmesini istedi.
Kestel'de bulunan yanmış insan kemikleri üzerinde yapılan incelemede, maksilla olarak adlandırılan üst çene kemiği parçasının diş yapısının Mehmet Şahinoğlu'nun 2011 yılındaki diş tedavisi kayıtlarıyla uyumlu olduğu belirlendi. Bursa 3. Ağır Ceza Mahkemesinin verdiği beraat kararları istinafta onandı. Ancak Yargıtay 1. Ceza Dairesi, 4 Şubat 2025 tarihinde beraat kararlarını eksik inceleme gerekçesiyle bozdu. Yargıtay, maksilla parçasının yanı sıra tanık ifadeleri ve HTS kayıtlarının ayrıntılı şekilde değerlendirilmesini istedi.
Yargıtay'ın bozma kararının ardından yeniden başlayan yargılamada, Mehmet Şahinoğlu'nu İstanbul'a çağırdığı öne sürülen Sultan D.'ye ulaşılamadı. Mayıs 2026'da hakkında yakalama kararı çıkarıldı. Dosyanın önemli isimlerinden İsmail Yazal'ın ise olaydan aylar sonra bir evde ölü bulunduğu ortaya çıktı. Mehmet Salih A.'nın adı, 2004 yılında kaybolan 21 yaşındaki Leyla Şakar dosyasındaki iddialarda da yer aldı. Leyla'nın öldürülmesinde Mehmet Salih A.'nın da parmağı olduğu öne sürüldü. Ancak genç kadının akıbeti 22 yıldır aydınlatılamadı.

Outsiders had little reason to notice when Nvidia’s longtime chief security officer and head of product security stepped down in August. Just two and a half months later, CEO Jensen Huang himself left the company over growing questions about his extramarital relationships — starting with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore data center company that U.S. investigators suspect of funneling Nvidia chips to China, then widening to reports about two separate affairs with Nvidia employees.
At the time, David Reber, who spent four years as CSO and seven at Nvidia overall, said he was leaving for health reasons. “This wasn’t a pivot I had planned. But I know what needs to come first: family and health,” he wrote on LinkedIn in late August, disclosing that he’d been diagnosed with young-onset Parkinson’s more than two years ago.
Reber’s replacement, Saša Zdjelar, previously spent 17 years at ExxonMobil in Houston, leaving as a senior IT manager before spending one year at Salesforce and several years at the cybersecurity company ReversingLabs. Zdjelar didn’t respond to questions Thursday about the transition or what the security team knew.
Nothing public connects Reber’s or Zdjelar’s role changes to the Megaspeed matter, but it seems fair to wonder what Nvidia’s security team knew about the government’s scrutiny of Megaspeed and about Huang’s relationships, and whether anyone raised concerns. Reber didn’t respond to questions Thursday. Nvidia also has not answered our related questions.
Relationships between a CEO and his employees typically fall to HR, legal and the board, not security. But security specialists say any affair — even one inside the office — can give a foreign intelligence service leverage over an exec who wants it kept quiet. And Huang’s relationship with an executive at Megaspeed, a company under federal investigation, wasn’t an office matter at all. (Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing.)
Still, spotting the clues isn’t easy. The way intelligence services collect information, much of it through everyday conversation rather than hacking, makes it especially difficult for security teams to identify risks, according to retired senior intelligence officer Nicholas Eftimiades, who says he has trained more than 1,000 corporate security professionals.
Some people inside Nvidia clearly knew parts of the picture. Nvidia’s top lawyer was engaged with the government’s Megaspeed inquiry more than a year ago, The New York Times reported earlier this week . (Nvidia has said it regularly contacts officials.) Reports about Huang’s relationships with employees suggest colleagues also knew of them, even if the behavior is not expressly forbidden by Nvidia’s code of conduct . The Times cited five Nvidia employees who said he was involved with a vice president who reported directly to him, and Reuters, citing two people, later reported a second relationship. What’s unclear is whether any of that reached security.
Even if it had reached Nvidia’s security team, Eftimiades, who wrote Chinese Espionage Operations and Tactics in 2020, said a security team’s resources are often limited. For one thing, they’re often underfunded because, unlike some other cost centers, they don’t drive revenue. It’s astonishingly common for CEOs to answer a security team’s warnings with “not a nickel more than compliance,” he said.
Many companies also define security overly narrowly, specialists say. In an opinion piece in The Hill , Don Aviv, CEO of the corporate investigations firm Interfor International, and author Jeremy Hurewitz, wrote, “Too many companies still approach security primarily as a matter of protecting facilities, preventing cyberattacks, and responding to physical threats.” The two argued that “[s]ecurity teams need to pay greater attention to insider threats, including the cultivation of executives and employees by foreign intelligence services, suspicious business relationships, conflicts of interest and attempts to obtain sensitive information through trusted personal contacts.”
It would be surprising if Nvidia’s security team didn’t have a more expansive remit than most companies given its scale and business partners, but it’s possible.
In fairness, some of it is simply beyond what any team can do. Speaking generally, not about Huang, Eftimiades offered a hypothetical in which a CEO complains that he can’t do something because “I’m fighting a board who doesn’t want to do this.” That tells an intelligence asset who the obstacle is. The service then asks, “Who’s the sticking point here?” and looks for ways into that person’s email and phone.
What a rival intelligence service wants is often less technology than policy insight, including who’s pushing to change export rules and who the biggest blocker is. “Intel world tends to be like cancer,” he said. “Once it gets into the body, it looks to spread and looks to reach out.”
The playbook isn’t new, Eftimiades added, “particularly for China.” Any executive dealing with the country “will tell you that they’ve been approached.” He said there are also “tons of diplomat stories” of U.S. diplomats walking into a hotel room to find a woman on the bed. He said what’s newer compared with Soviet era spying is the relationships these services cultivate now often last years, not weeks.
Technology can augment that human intelligence, Eftimiades said, pointing to IMSI catchers as one example. The devices mimic a cell tower so that nearby phones connect to them. A basic version can cost about $1,000 and fit in a suitcase, he said, though government-grade models cost far more, and there were a couple of cases involving Chinese espionage where these factored in last year.
Eftimiades says no one knows yet if the devices were used against Huang, whose phone was presumably hardened such that compromises could be detected, if not stopped altogether. But what Nvidia’s security team knew, and whether it could have acted on it, will only become clearer as the board’s independent investigation and federal inquiries proceed.
In the meantime, Eftimiades said he hopes the whole episode is “a wake-up call” for U.S. industry, which he said is mostly “clueless” about China’s tactics. “We have lost trillions [of dollars] in intellectual property,” is his guess. “Whatever we think we’re doing isn’t working.”

All configurations of the Mac Mini are on sale today on Amazon, starting at $779 for the base M6 model . That's $120 off the full retail price that Apple charges.
For nearly half of this year, the Mac Mini was unavailable to buy; it was either sold out at retailers or subject to wait times that stretched up to three months long . But at the end of August, Apple launched a new model, which not only introduced the M6 (or M5 Pro ) chip inside, but also restocked the Mac Mini so that you can actually just go out and buy one.
The sharp escalation in demand even took Apple by surprise , by its own admission. AI enthusiasts were buying these up for the quick and simple access to an always-on computer with enough memory to run models locally in an affordable package.
The M6 comes with 16 GB of RAM, which is barely enough to run some smaller models. Amazon also sells a 24-GB model (with 512 GB of storage) for $1,150. If you want to bump up the storage capability to 32 GB, you'll have to buy the machine directly from Apple. Either way, the extra storage will make your Mini quite a bit more expensive than the base model, but it's still $150 off the retail price. Best Buy is also selling the previous-gen M4 model for $649 if you're really trying to save cash—or just need a basic computer for work. The M6 does offer a substantial upgrade to GPU performance over the M4, though, so if you're planning to do any on-device AI work, it's worth the extra $120.
I should note that this isn't the lowest price I've seen the Mac Mini reach—though it's close. For one day in October, it dropped by an extra $10. I can't say for sure whether we'll see an additional price decrease during Black Friday. My gut says no, but if you're worried about it, you might want to put it in your shopping cart and wait before clicking “purchase.”
The best deal in the Mac world heading into Black Friday, however, is the M5 MacBook Air . It's currently $1,099 , and that still gets you 16 GB of unified memory.

A petition calling on Nvidia to reinstate the company’s recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang appears to have attracted more than 115,000 signatures as of Saturday afternoon.
The petition website said the signers include 5,965 current Nvidia employees, 1,108 former employees, and 63,063 shareholders. Notable supporters include Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan.
The petition states that its signers are “concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process” and demands that the board “bring him back while an independent investigation establishes the facts.” It also calls on the board to ensure a fair investigation and provide more information to the public.
“Jensen deserves due process, not mob justice,” the petition says.
Huang resigned on Thursday , four days after confessing to having an affair with a chip executive suspected by U.S. intelligence to be a Chinese spy. The former CEO has agreed to testify before Congress, while news reports have also suggested that Huang engaged in multiple extramarital affairs .
Nvidia appointed CFO Colette Kress as the company’s interim CEO while it searches for a permanent replacement. Nvidia’s stock price fell sharply through the week, while Huang’s departure is also expected to leave a big gap in AI industry funding .

Sometimes new species evade detection because they’re tiny and thus easy to miss—not this giant fungus. Shaped like a hand reaching out of the ground, this new species of fungus was discovered deep in the forest in China’s Yunnan Province. A research team from the Kunming Institute of Botany, part of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, reported it as a new species they named Dianjunus rex .
The name comes from the region’s ancient Dian Kingdom and the Chinese pronunciation of the word “fungus.” D. rex is a type of Ascomycete, which is the largest phylum of fungi with over 64,000 known species, and among them, this new fungus produces the largest masses of mushroom recorded. Unlike what we typically think of as a “mushroom,” Ascomycetes don’t form caps and stems but produce structures called fruiting bodies, which release spores to reproduce. And growing up to 20 inches and weighting nearly five pounds, D. rex ’s are huge.
Within the Ascomycetes, the giant fungus constitutes an entirely new biological family (the broader classification of genus and species), meaning that it has no close relatives—at least that we know of. While 6,000 fungal species have been documented in Yunnan, mycologists believe the province known for its biological diversity could easily harbor 100,000
“The discovery illustrates how much fungus biodiversity remains to be discovered in East Asian forests,” Indunil C. Senanayake, an associate professor at the Kunming Institute of Botany and the lead author of the paper, said in a press release .
Senanayake and his research team conducted surveys in the Nanban tropical rainforest, where they came across large, whitish fruiting bodies growing in the soil near the roots of dying trees. They documented and collected fungi growing in a wide variety of shapes like cylinders, spindles, and cupped palms. The fruiting bodies appeared to develop finger-like branches upon maturity. They found that the above-ground portions are covered with white, powdery fibers that turn dark yellow as the fungi mature while the portions buried in the soil are black and smooth.
The fruiting bodies dried rapidly when the scientists took samples back to the lab. They found that the interiors were dense and sponge-like, appearing white or yellow with no strong odor or taste. (Don’t try this experiment at home.)
Analyzing the DNA of these fungi, the researchers reconstructed a “molecular clock,” which revealed that D. rex diverged from other species approximately 65 million years ago. This is the end of the Cretaceous period, immediately following the mass extinction that is believed to have wiped out three quarters of all plant and animal species, including the dinosaurs. That means D. rex and T. rex never met, but this era was likely a boon for fungi . Large quantities of dead plant material became available following the die off, which could have provided new ecological opportunities for fungi and other organisms that decompose such matter.
Genomic analyses, however, indicated that D. rex doesn’t have nearly as many decomposition-related genes as the scientists expected. Compared to some of its closest relatives that also feast on plant matter, the huge fungus has only about half the usual number of decomposition-related genes.
Senanayake has a theory about this. Though, so far, they have only found the fruiting bodies around dying plants, the fungus may be leading a “double life”— living inside healthy trees and then feeding on dead plant material when the hosts die . That could perhaps explain how D. rex is able to store enough energy to build the massive fruiting bodies.
This is just a theory for now, but the giant fungi undoubtedly do need a surplus of energy to grow so large. Senanayake hypothesizes that the benefit of these large fruiting bodies is that they tower higher than the surrounding plants and fallen leaves, which could be advantageous for wind-mediated spore dispersal in a dense forest. “However, such a large structure requires substantial energy investment, suggesting that this strategy likely evolved only where the ecological benefits outweighed the costs.”
This story was originally published in WIRED Japan and has been translated from Japanese.

These are two threat models for which disk encryption is the answer:
The device is stolen or lost and its contents must remain secret.
The device is tampered with, and all attempts at tampering must render it unusable.
Right now, we will focus on the first threat model. It is very difficult to build a tamper-proof system, and you need to worry about tamper-proofing your hardware, depending on what kind of actor is a realistic threat.
If we want to keep data on the system secret, we must first consider which data is worth protecting. On a NetBSD system, our data can be grouped into two broad categories:
Does the /bin/sh executable downloaded from the NetBSD FTP server contain any sensitive information?
On a BSD system, due to the separation of the base system and packages, many root file system directories are mostly unmodified outside of upgrades. In a properly configured system, nearly all system daemons and user applications are not going to be running as root , so won’t have permission to modify or create files in /bin .
We can reasonably assume that /bin/sh is the same binary that every other NetBSD user is running. A user may even opt to make directories containing such system files read-only.
The operating system needs to be able to load files to boot. [citation needed] This makes "true" full disk encryption difficult to achieve without specialized hardware, since the user needs some way to enter a password or an encryption key, and can’t do so without some form of software running on their computer. NetBSD also needs to store some amount of metadata about the encrypted partition on the disk, such as information on how to generate a secure 256-bit key from a 24 character password.
It is common for Unix systems to use shared libraries, which are loaded by programs to access system functionality. If these become unavailable, for example, by /usr/lib going missing, it becomes much harder to use the system. Familiarize yourself with the standard utilities in /rescue which don’t need working shared libraries to be useful.
The cryptographic algorithms that get standardized by the US government tend to be slow when implemented in software . This carries a performance penalty. As a result, many modern CPUs include implementations of ciphers like AES in hardware. For those that don’t, there’s alternative ciphers like Adiantum .
On a normal NetBSD system, several directories have a high chance of being modified during system operation:
/var - log files, system-wide databases (e.g. mail notifications), crash dumps…
/root - configuration files relevant to the root user account
/usr/pkg and /usr/local - where third-party software is installed
/etc - init scripts, system-wide configuration for the base system
A simple approach might be to encrypt /home . However, this might not be enough for some users. Although the crash directory can be easily changed with sysctl , a crash dump contains a snapshot of system memory which might be sensitive. If any servers have been run on the system, the log files might be sensitive. Mail sent to users (e.g. about their interrupted vi sessions and associated backups) might reveal sensitive file names.
Some users opt for the cgdroot approach, which uses only a small unencrypted ramdisk to pivot to an encrypted file system. However, this modifies the system startup routines significantly and may make certain rescue options harder. So, it’s worth asking whether there’s an approach that is somewhere in the middle, and still uses the standard NetBSD installation and boot process. Many BSD systems use separate file system partitions for /usr and /var , and this is a standard configuration supported by the NetBSD installer.
/etc is a harder problem to solve, since it contains files necessary to boot the system. However, on a typical desktop system, many files in /etc remain untouched. Passwords in /etc are generally stored only in hash form, except for Wi-Fi access points and certain VPN configurations (although it’s easy to reconfigure wpa_supplicant_flags to use a different configuration file from the default one in /etc ). Many configuration files are only loaded much later in the boot process, after /usr is already mounted, and can easily be replaced with symbolic links to files on another file system.
The NetBSD installer has basic functionality, but gets the job done quickly. In this configuration, we’re going to install NetBSD to a small unencrypted root file system. When you start to ignore the growth that can occur in /usr and /var and /home , even a complete NetBSD installation with development tools included is tiny. 4 GB should be more than enough.
For example purposes, I am going to use a sparc64 virtual machine, but the process is basically the same for more mainstream CPU architectures like amd64.
The installer detects that we already have a partitioned disk. We’re going to pick the "e: Delete everything" option so we have a fresh disk to start with:
Next, we’re going to choose "Set sizes of NetBSD partitions". This will allow us to have a small root, and reserve a large encrypted partition:
Here, I’ve decided I want a 4096 MB (4 GB) root file system, and a 11263 MB (11 GB) partition allocated for /var . Later, we’ll make /usr and /var share a disk partition, so don’t worry about this too much. Select "Go on".
On the next screen, I’ve changed the type of the secondary partition to "cgd" (listed under "Other type"), NetBSD’s encrypted device driver. I’ve also set its mount point to "-" so we can reconfigure it later:
I tell the installer I want to do a Full Installation and it completes as normal, installing everything into the small root partition.
When we reboot and log in as root , we enter a new world… our 4 GB unencrypted root partition.
Since I’m on sparc64, the disk is partitioned into disklabels. wd0 is the primary drive, and the disklabel command shows that /dev/wd0d is the partition reserved for our encrypted file system:
We can go directly ahead with creating a parameters file for the cgd :
Now cgd0 appears to the system as yet another disk, but all attempts to access that disk will be automatically encrypted/decrypted by the kernel.
The next time we enter our password, we want to be able to verify that the password was correct, to avoid reading or writing invalid data.
This is done by choosing a verification method based on the contents of the encrypted partition. For flexibility’s sake, we’re going to put another disklabel inside the encrypted partition. This will allow the system to easily verify the password is correct by looking for a valid disklabel, but also gives us flexibility in our choice of file system.
This opens the interactive editor. We’re going to enter N to set a name for our disklabel (enter something like "cgdlabel"), then enter a to modify the first sub-partition.
First, it asks for a file system type. Enter ? to display a list of types:
Since I’m running -current and want to test the Log File System, I’m going to enter "4.4LFS". A more common and well-tested configuration would be "4.2BSD".
Since "a" is the only sub-partition at the moment, the default start of 0 is fine. "$" will use all available space on the cgd.
Finally, we’ll save our new label and quit the disklabel editor:
Now change the verify_method in /etc/cgd/wd0d to disklabel , and add a line in /etc/cgd/cgd.conf to create the cgd at boot time:
We can now access this hidden partition as /dev/cgd0a . But for it to be useful, we’ll need to create a file system on it. Once again, here I’m using the Log File System:
A more normal and well-tested configuration would be FFSv2ea:
Use "ffs" instead of "lfs" if you aren’t using the Log File System. If using FFS, you may want to use the options rw,log,noatime to enable journaling.

Today , along with the ACLU, EFF filed an amicus brief in the Sixth Circuit court of appeals in United States v. Sturdivant , a case where police warrantlessly tracked a suspect’s movements using Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) data. Our brief details the vast, interconnected network of ALPRs that constantly track drivers around the country and argues that this tracking is a “search” under the meaning of the Fourth Amendment.
Sturdivant involves a series of robberies in and around Cleveland, Ohio. Using surveillance camera footage, police identified the make, model, and color of the robber’s car, but they did not know its license plate number. After running an open-ended search of two ALPR databases, Flock and ELSAG, officers learned a car belonging to the defendant had been tracked near sites of the robberies, eventually leading to his arrest. Faced with a motion to suppress the ALPR evidence, the district court held that Mr. Sturdivant had no reasonable expectation of privacy in his license plate number because it could be observed by members of the public, and that therefore he had no Fourth Amendment interest in not having his car tracked in public places.
But ALPRs are simply not comparable to observing an individual license plate on a passing car. As we’ve explained in many amicus briefs and in our lawsuits directly challenging ALPR use in San Jose, California and Wisconsin , ALPRs give law enforcement “ a virtual time machine to view suspects’, or anyone else’s, past movements (and much more) with just the click of a button.” Just last month, a federal district court agreed and held that ALPRs are a “ form of indiscriminate mass surveillance” that can violate the Fourth Amendment.
We hope the Sixth Circuit will reverse the lower court in this case and hold that ALPR searches require a warrant.
This post was co-written by Andi Cao , an EFF legal intern. Automated license plate readers (ALPRs) are mass surveillance. They photograph every passing car and log where and when it was captured, building a searchable record of where nearly everyone drives. Cities should not buy them , and cities that...

We are in the middle of the Second ReNESance (the first one is the one that saved the video game industry in North America). The combined decades of research and knowledge on how the venerable little NES works have produced a true cornucopia of games. We are all lucky to be here to witness it.
I am always happy to inform video game fans that the Nintendo Entertainment System is still receiving lots and lots of new third-party games.
In alphabetical order, because I refuse to rank them, here are 25 of my favourite modern NES games. Almost all can be obtained digitally, usually from the developer or publisher, most for a modest fee. Digital NES downloads are cheap! Most of these can also be obtained as physical cartridges for the true hi-fi experience on original hardware.
Made by 8-bit Slasher who has been honing his skills in other horror games for the NES, All Hell Unleashed is an extensive love letter to the horror slashers of the 1980s and 1990s. There is an underlying story about an evil cult that is trying to resurrect something or other, but that’s just an excuse plot so that you can fight Jaws, Freddy, Jason, Ghostface and others. It works surprisingly well. You can select your favourite horror movie from a stage-select screen to do your platforming as you fight the forces of evil, culminating in the boss fights where the villain of each horror franchise swoops in for a mano-a-mano . The platforming feels good, and the boss fights function as set pieces showcasing the real villains we are here to see in their 8-bit glory.
Finally Jason dons a better outfit on the NES than that silly purple jumpsuit!
After each classic horror villain is defeated, it is time to take on the cult itself for one final showdown. Definitely a spine-tingling adventure!
Alwa’s Awakening was originally a PC game made with pseudo-NES limitations (and in the case of the music, with actual NES limitations, as the developer used Famitracker to compose all of the music). If it doesn’t feel like a classic NES game and instead plays more like a modern indie Metroidvania, that’s because it is.
In the game, you play as Zoe, a girl who likes video games and one day awakens in the mystical land of Alwa, a place from one of her games. Your task is to guide Zoe through an adventure in Alwa where she will uncover power-ups that open up new avenues of adventure. Typical Metroidvania stuff, although a bit shorter than most games in the genre. The PC-to-NES port of this game was handled by my good friend Brad Smith of Lizard fame. He made a couple of interesting YouTube videos describing the process.
The game looks absolutely gorgeous for the NES, and its Famitracker-composed soundtrack made it through the porting process completely unscathed. There was a limited physical edition that today is only available via secondhand markets. If you can grab a copy, it’s a very high-quality production. This is some of the best stuff made for the system.
Anguna is an NES game with an interesting lineage. It was originally made in 2008 for the Game Boy Advance as essentially the same game, but a bit more to the standards of the GBA. Then it was successively ported to the Nintendo DS, the Atari 2600, and finally the NES.
The Atari 2600-to-NES port was done fairly faithfully, which means that the design decisions necessary for the Atari also made it into the NES port. This means, for example, no more than two enemies per screen and always of the same type. This sort of restriction isn’t unheard of in the NES, though. The very popular NES Double Dragon port also has the same limitation. The game design makes up for it and overall results in an enjoyable experience. And isn’t that what making and playing modern NES games is all about? An interesting experience made with strict hardware limitations.
So what is Anguna? At its most basic, it’s a Zelda-like. You walk around screens, you grab new tools, your tools open new paths for exploration, you use the tools to fight monsters, with the most common tool in question being your trusty sword. You are a nameless warrior who is notably NOT called “Anguna” on a quest to defeat the goblin king. Usual bare-bones plot.
Most might consider this game to be short, but I would say it’s sleek and streamlined. It doesn’t do much, but what it does it does well.
Oh, one very important upgrade that the game got during the 2600-to-NES conversion: rockin’ enemy portraits in gorgeous 8-bit pixel art!
Blazing Rangers is single-screen arcade firefighting co-op action! The firefighting genre is under-explored in video games and Blazing Rangers manages to represent it admirably.
The goal is to rescue the children in each burning level and proceed to the next one. To do this you have to snake a powerful firehose that can blast both flames and baddies as you make your way to the children. You may also and often must drop your firehose and rely on your backpack with water in order to get to the further reaches of each level. There are powerups to collect, which give bonuses such as increasing the length of the hose or activating a sprinkler system that will slow the spread of fire throughout the level.
You can control either of two characters, Popo and Mimi, each with slight differences in gameplay. Popo is a bit slower but can recharge his backpack with water faster while Mimi is the other way around. Each level is timed, but you’re more likely to be overrun by flames or enemies than running out of time. The children can get singed by the fire but otherwise seem unharmed, unless you get burned carrying them, in which case they get burned too.
The game has a very catchy theme song that is also the BGM of each level.
Although it can be fun enough in single player, co-op is where the game really excels. It is very fun to coordinate with your partner as there is still only one hose in co-op. A strategy, for example, could be to have one player get the hose extension powerup that the other player can instantly use to take the hose a bit further into the flames.
Estique is a horizontal shmup with the distinct honour of being made by some of the original Compile developers, veterans of the shmup genre. This is noticeable in that it even uses some sound effects from Compile classics such as The Guardian Legend . In the game you pilot the eponymous super-robot that can transform between the bipedal mecha form that can recover damage more quickly or a sleek spaceship form that is more manoeuvrable and has a faster firing rate. Gameplay consists of carefully balancing between the two forms in the heat of battle depending on whether a more offensive or defensive approach is needed at the time.
The NES manual has a deliberately awkward English translation as a homage to the quality of writing we often encountered during the licensed era. Accordingly, the Japanese and English versions of the game are not identical, with the English version having mild censorship of the cut scenes, mimicking the restrictions that Nintendo used to impose on licensed NES games.
The game’s default difficulty is a little on the easy side, and the whole game can be completed in under an hour at the default difficulty. I get the impression that the intended difficulty is a bit higher, so you can always adjust it up for your gaming needs.
Regardless of the difficulty, the giant screen-filling boss fights are always a delight.
Why 2nd adventure, you might ask? Well, this game has an interesting history . The original adventure was written way back in 2015 to support the Arc of Cowlitz County charity. Within a couple of years, a sequel appeared and physical copies were made and distributed at the Portland Retro Gaming Expo. They aren’t made anymore, but if you’re exceedingly lucky, you might be able to nab a second-hand copy somewhere. Finally the game was uploaded to itch.io as a free download, with a nudge to donate to the charity.
The game is a tightly-made single-screen arcade platformer where siblings Kaylee and J…

Three men have been convicted of carrying out an attack on a church in the Karak governorate that killed nine people.
A Jordanian court has sentenced three men to death by hanging for carrying out last month’s deadly gun attack on a church in the kingdom’s south.
Armed men killed nine people and wounded 25 others, storming a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in Hammoud village, in the Karak governorate on October 23.

“One of the perpetrators of the terrorist operation was also convicted of providing funds with the intention of using them to finance the commission of terrorist acts,” it added.
In late October, Jordanian security forces arrested the three suspects in the attack on St George’s Greek Orthodox church after clashing with them.
The governorate is home to many members of Jordan’s Christian minority, which makes up about 300,000 of the country’s 11.5 million people.
King Abdullah II said those behind the attack would face the “harshest penalties” as he offered his condolences to the victims’ families. He has ordered a review of the country’s security procedures for responding to attacks after the incident.
texts.https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3rr:
Nine people were killed in the shooting at the Greek Orthodox church last month
A Jordanian court has sentenced three men to death by hanging for carrying out a fatal mass shooting on a church last month.
The attack on 23 October killed nine people and injured 34 others who had been attending a Christian funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak governorate.
Jordan's Armed Forces said in a statement on Sunday that the men had been convicted of committing "terrorist acts", as well as possessing weapons, "promoting the ideas of a terrorist organisation" and "conspiracy to commit terrorist acts".
The three men - two Jordanian brothers and their brother-in-law - fled the scene of the attack and were arrested three days later. They have not been publicly identified.
Karak is home to a sizeable Christian community in the Muslim-majority kingdom.
CCTV footage from the day of the attack showed three men holding guns approaching and firing on St George's church in the village of Hmoud.
A second video showed dead and wounded people lying on the ground amid chaotic scenes at the church.
It is still unclear why the attackers chose to target that specific church.
Shortly after the attack, Jordan's King Abdullah II wrote on X: "The terrorist attack against Karak will be met with the harshest retaliation.
"Those who delude themselves into thinking that they can divide Jordanians with their bullets have no chance in the face of our unity."
The three men fled the scene of the shooting and were later located inside an abandoned house in Karak governorate, south of the capital, Amman.
They refused to surrender and opened fire on security forces, who returned fire and wounded all three of them , the Public Security Directorate said at the time. No security personnel were hurt in the shootout.
King Abdullah praised security forces for chasing the suspects "to the very end".
The week after the Karak shooting, Jordan struck what its military said were "terrorist organisations" in Syria in retaliation to the church attack.

Executions in Jordan are carried out by hanging. The kingdom previously observed an unofficial ban on executions from 2006 to 2014, and another pause from 2017 until June this year.

Judge Noël Wise found buyers plausibly alleged the chipmakers conspired to cut conventional DRAM supply and shift capacity to HBM, distinguishing the Ninth Circuit's DRAM II.
A federal judge on Nov. 14 refused to dismiss a proposed class action accusing Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron of conspiring to restrict the supply of conventional dynamic random-access memory, or DRAM, the standardized memory chips used in computers, phones and servers.
U.S. District Judge Noël Wise of the Northern District of California denied the companies' joint motion to dismiss in full, finding the complaint plausibly alleged an agreement in violation of Section 1 of the Sherman Act. The allegations, accepted as true at this stage, have not been proven.
The companies argued the case was a rerun of DRAM II, in which the Ninth Circuit in 2022 affirmed dismissal of claims against the same three companies over a 2016–2018 supply restriction. "The Court finds that it is not," Judge Wise wrote.
The suit was filed June 25, 2026, by 17 consumers and small businesses from five states. It concerns conventional DRAM, which the complaint describes as "standardized memory built to industry specifications and sold for ordinary purposes," including DDR5 generation modules built for computers.
According to the complaint, the three companies controlled more than 91% of global DRAM revenue as of the third quarter of 2025. They allegedly cut production starting in late 2022 and, beginning in 2023, shifted capacity to high bandwidth memory, or HBM, a specialized DRAM product for artificial intelligence accelerators that "requires approximately three to four times the silicon wafer area per gigabyte compared to conventional DDR5 DRAM."
By the third quarter of 2025, conventional DRAM prices had risen 171.8% in one year, according to the complaint, which alleges a 697% increase over 18 months. Yet "not one of the three Defendants expanded or announced plans to meaningfully expand commodity DRAM production capacity," the complaint alleges.
Without direct evidence of an agreement, the plaintiffs needed plus factors, additional facts suggesting a preceding agreement rather than conscious parallelism, in which competitors independently make similar moves.
Judge Wise rejected the companies' argument that timing gaps undercut parallel action. SK Hynix and Micron announced cuts three weeks apart in late 2022, she noted, and Samsung's lag of about four and a half months, until April 7, 2023, was "not such an unreasonably long delay that it defeats an allegation of parallel conduct on a motion to dismiss."
She found the complaint plausibly alleged that the three companies acted in parallel when they cut supply, shifted production from conventional DRAM such as DDR5 to HBM, and wound down DDR4.
Under Ninth Circuit precedent, action against self-interest must be "so perilous in the absence of advance agreement that no reasonable firm would make the challenged move without such an agreement." Judge Wise wrote that a pivot to HBM by itself "might not be sufficient," but that "the related conduct tips this factor over the edge to weigh in Plaintiffs' favor."
According to the complaint, all three signed long-term contracts locking in HBM supply, Samsung and SK Hynix reportedly refused long-term agreements with major conventional DRAM customers, and Micron announced on Dec. 3, 2025, that it would close Crucial, its 30-year-old consumer brand. Those moves, which she called "difficult if not impossible to unwind," plus the failure to expand despite record prices, "are the sort that at the pleading stage, it appears no reasonable firm would make without a prior agreement," she wrote.
She applied similar reasoning to allegations that Samsung and Micron delayed or halted new DRAM plants, citing the Ninth Circuit's 1990 Petroleum Products decision that "Changes in refinery capacity are not readily reversible." "The Court views the commitment to build or not build manufacturing capacity as analogous," she wrote. She also counted the companies' alleged same-quarter 2025 decisions to wind down DDR4 as a plus factor, citing the complaint's allegation that "older, slower DDR4 came to cost more per gigabyte than newer, faster DDR5."
Judge Wise found that near-identical customer-vetting practices all three companies allegedly adopted in January 2026 "strongly support a plausible inference of conspiracy." She rejected the companies' "obvious and non-conspiratorial explanation" of booming AI demand, noting that the vetting began after the AI boom and the HBM pivot were underway.
The court gave no weight to three other arguments. Judge Wise held that investor statements, including Micron's 2022 reference to "supply discipline," did not distinguish the case from DRAM II. Though the conference-meeting allegations went beyond those in DRAM II, she wrote that DRAM II "seemingly all but forecloses a trial court from giving any weight to trade conference meetings" absent specifics, and she called the market's oligopolistic structure "neutral in the analysis."
According to the complaint, the companies and two other manufacturers formed a criminal cartel to fix DRAM prices from 1998 to 2002; Samsung paid a $300 million fine, Hynix paid $185 million, and Micron received immunity for cooperating as a whistleblower. Judge Wise, like the DRAM II court, rejected the argument that the now-20-year-old history should not count.
At the hearing, the companies quoted the late Judge Posner's line that competitors in concentrated markets "watch each other like hawks." Judge Wise wrote: "But Plaintiffs' allegations go beyond hawks watching each other; their contentions are more akin to hawks flying in formation – an activity that hawks ordinarily do not do."
The plaintiffs are represented by Bathaee Dunne LLP. Samsung is represented by O'Melveny & Myers LLP, SK Hynix by Cleary Gottlieb Steen & Hamilton LLP, and Micron by Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher LLP.
Judge Wise ordered the companies to answer by Dec. 7, 2026. Because the court had reset argument by about three weeks, she also granted the companies' unopposed administrative motion to continue early case deadlines and reset the initial case management conference for Jan. 12, 2027, at 9 a.m.

The Bahrain Defence Force says its air defence systems thwart several Iranian ‘aerial attacks’.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says it has launched six drones at a US air defence radar system at Bahrain’s Riffa Air Base in response to what it describes as hostile US actions.
Sirens sounded in Bahrain on Sunday as its Ministry of Interior urged residents to “remain calm” and “proceed to the nearest safe location”. It was the second time in three days that the IRGC claimed to have targeted a US radar system in Bahrain.
The US military said it intercepted two Iranian drones on Friday but has yet to comment on Sunday’s claim.
The IRGC said it struck the radar at Bahrain’s Riffa Air Base, according to a statement carried by the IRGC-affiliated Fars News Agency.
Bahrain’s Interior Ministry issued two alerts within about three hours, the first about 4:30am (01:30 GMT). The ministry warned of a “potential threat” and urged residents to seek shelter. It gave no further details about the threat.
The Bahrain Defence Force also said its air defence systems thwarted several Iranian “aerial attacks” targeting the kingdom.
In its statement, the IRGC said the Strait of Hormuz remained closed and claimed that US efforts to escort ships through the waterway had failed. It warned that any US attack would draw a more severe response.
The IRGC said on Friday that it destroyed a US early-warning radar system in Bahrain in retaliation for what it described as an air attack on a telecommunications tower in southern Iran. The US military’s Central Command (CENTCOM) denied the claim, saying it had shot down two IRGC drones and there were no injuries or damage.
In a statement carried by Iran’s semiofficial Tasnim News Agency, the IRGC called the operation a “serious warning” over what it described as aerial provocations and oil smuggling in the Strait of Hormuz. Reuters reported that Friday marked the first time since early September that Iran had claimed an attack on US military assets in a Gulf country.
Tehran has told the United Nations Security Council it would respond immediately to renewed US or Israeli attacks and has accused Bahrain and other Gulf states of supporting US military operations. Bahrain has called for the full implementation of Security Council Resolution 2817, which condemned Iranian attacks on Bahrain and other countries in the region and demanded they stop.
Manama, Bahrain, is where the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet is based. A Pentagon inspector general’s report released in September found that Iranian attacks had damaged or destroyed buildings at US installations in eight countries, including Bahrain, in the first four months of the US-Israel war on Iran, which began on February 28.
The IRGC’s navy said two oil tankers struck sea mines on Saturday while trying to pass through the Strait of Hormuz. In a statement carried by Iran’s state news agency IRNA, it said the vessels had switched off their navigation and tracking systems and were using what it called an “unauthorised” route.
The IRGC said two other tankers turned back towards the Gulf after receiving warnings from its maritime traffic control centre.
Reporting from Tehran, Al Jazeera’s Mohammed Vall said on Saturday that there were “two similar incidents yesterday” and the number of tankers hitting mines has increased.
Vall said Iran claims that the Strait of Hormuz is under its “full control” and “only Iran and Oman have the right to control it”. The United States rejects that claim.
According to Vall, Iran blamed the incidents on the tanker owners and the countries backing them, saying they had failed to comply with the regulations Iran imposed on passage through the strait.
Diplomatic efforts to stop attacks and reopen the Strait of Hormuz remain stalled with Iran’s parliamentary speaker and chief negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, telling Al Jazeera that Tehran wanted to move beyond a state of “no war, no peace”.
Ghalibaf said in the interview last week that Iran has conveyed seven conditions for a deal through a Qatari mediator and was awaiting an official US response. The conditions he outlined included lifting the US naval blockade and sanctions, releasing frozen Iranian funds, ending hostilities on all fronts and formally declaring the war over.
US President Donald Trump’s administration, meanwhile, has tightened sanctions and maintained the blockade on Iranian ports.
Saeid Golkar, the UC Foundation associate professor of political science at the University of Tennessee at Chattanooga, told Al Jazeera that limited exchanges could escalate into a wider war.
“Both sides may prefer to avoid a full-scale war, but the danger lies in miscalculation,” Golkar said.
“Iran may continue limited maritime and regional escalation to increase pressure while Washington could respond militarily. Such exchanges could eventually lead to a broader conflict that neither side initially intended.”

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of the fighting in the Middle East.
Iran has targeted an airbase in Bahrain in the latest resumption of strikes since September, prompting public warnings and sirens to ring out in the Gulf kingdom this morning.
According to Iranian media, the IRGC said it had sent six drones to attack a US radar system hosted in the US-allied island state.
Explosions were heard around the capital, Manama, but Bahrain authorities say their air defences intercepted the attacks before they reached their targets.
Bahrain, which lies directly across the Persian Gulf from Iran, is home to the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet, and has been repeatedly attacked by Tehran during the course of the war, which has seen flare-ups in strikes amid long bouts of inaction.

Negotiations to end the war remain at a stalemate, with the US maintaining its naval blockade and Iran its stranglehold over the strait of Hormuz.
Developments in the Red Sea this morning will add to further concerns for Gulf oil flows.

Elsewhere, Hamas has confirmed that a senior commander involved in planning the 7 October attacks was killed in an Israeli airstrike on Saturday.
The US thinks Iran still has between 1,500-2,500 missiles in its arsenal despite the US-Israeli damage done this year to its production facilities, reports the Wall St Journal.
That’s the “low confidence” assessment from intelligence analysts, the American paper reports, citing US officials.
They noted difficulties with tracking Iran’s stockpile, and assessing whether they’re ready for launch or remain in storage.
But they noted that Iran has appeared to manage to slowly rebuild its arsenal during the long lulls in fighting and mostly from stockpiled weapons components. Tehran has also kept up a ready supply of drones and short-range missiles.

Here’s a recap of what the various sides have said this morning regarding the latest Iranian strikes targeting a US air base in Bahrain .
double quotation mark The US air defence radar system at the Al-Riffa helicopter base in Bahrain was targeted by six drones belonging to the IRGC Aerospace Force.
The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and any aggression by the American enemy will be met with an even harsher and more forceful response.
double quotation mark Iran continues its systematic hostile approach through its sinful attacks targeting the Kingdom of Bahrain. [Bahrain] rejects turning its territory into an arena for settling scores and holds Iran fully responsible for these attacks.
I’m yet to see a response from the US, but can expect Centcomm (which oversees all American military operations in the Middle East) to comment at some stage, like it did for Friday’s attack . Those strikes also targeted a radar site.
After two months of calm, the explosions have started again for Bahrain citizens.
Locals reported hearing blasts about 4am local time, and then a second round at 6.30am.
double quotation mark It’s exactly what I was hoping wouldn’t happen: Iranian attacks starting again, with all the worry and uncertainty that go with them”, Hayat Ibrahim, 65, told AFP news agency.
Another resident, Mohammed Abdallah, a shopkeeper in the capital Manama, which is just north of the air base targeted said:
double quotation mark I was hoping this period was behind us and wouldn’t happen again.
Bahrain’s Interior Ministry posted public warnings on X, telling “residents to remain calm, proceed to the nearest safe location, and follow news through official channels”.
Iran had last launched strikes in the first week of September, when the regime targeted US military assets in Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates and Kuwait.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said they had launched six drones targeting a US air defence radar at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base on Sunday morning, reported Iranian media.
They said they had attacked the air base in retaliation for “hostile US actions”. The base is about a 30-minute drive south of Manama.
US forces have been quietly carrying out a series of strikes on Iranian sites in recent weeks, including on the key Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, where there’s a major IRGC presence. Trump has called them minor strikes. Bahrain officials this morning have accused Tehran of continuing a “systematic hostile approach” to the kingdom.
The drone flurry this morning comes just 48 hours after Iran launched drones on Friday, the first escalations targeting Bahrain in two months.
That attack targeted an American radar facility. US Central Command said it had shot down the two drones without any injury or damage.
Bahrain officials hadn’t issued any warnings for that attack, but were forced to send out public alerts this morning telling residents to seek shelter. The Interior Ministry told locals to remain calm but proceed to to the nearest safe location.

gawain requires type annotations on the variables, parameters, returns and class attributes of Python code, then runs a type checker, ty or pyrefly , to check that the types are correct.
Type checkers such as mypy, Pyright, ty and pyrefly infer the type of a variable that has no annotation. ruff's ANN rules and flake8-annotations ask for annotations on functions only. gawain also asks for them on variables and class attributes.
I built gawain only because I hate dict[str, Any] and wanted to do something about it. If your answer to this is "but Python already infers that" or "but my IDE infers it for me", then don't use it, little padawan.
retries = 3 passes, because a literal has an obvious type. PORT is a constant, so it needs Final[int] .
When every annotation is in place, gawain runs the type checker on the same files and prints what it reports. With ty, the default, for prices.py :
Install gawain with the extra of the type checker you want. ty is the default checker, and the ty extra pins it to 0.0.100:
To use pyrefly instead, install the pyrefly extra, which pins pyrefly 1.4.1 and does not install ty:
Then choose it with checker = "pyrefly" in [tool.gawain] , or with --checker pyrefly . docs/configuration.md explains the switch.
pip install gawain without an extra installs only the gawain command. It then needs a checker on PATH , or --no-types to run the annotation checks only.
Use gawain with care. ty is in beta, and its diagnostics may change between versions. If that is a problem for your project, use pyrefly, or --no-types to run the annotation checks only.
gawain exits with 0 when nothing is reported, 1 when it reports an error, and 2 on a usage error or when the type checker cannot run. The type checker's warnings are printed but do not fail the check.
GW000 marks a file gawain cannot read, and GW900 and GW901 mark a broken or unused suppression. To silence a line, name the code:
docs/rules.md has the full rules, the exemptions and the suppression syntax.
The default mode is obvious . A name may go without an annotation when its value has an obvious type and the name is never assigned again: a literal ( count = 0 ), a container of literals ( ids = [1, 2, 3] ) or a constructor call ( user = User("ada") ). strict asks for an annotation on every assignment:
pre-commit installs the hook from this repository's source, so building it needs Rust 1.97 or newer. docs/configuration.md covers [tool.gawain] , paths and the hook in detail.
On the CPython 3.14 standard library (1,847 files, 974,586 lines), median of 30 runs (5 for flake8-annotations):
gawain ran with --no-types . This is one benchmark on one machine (AMD Ryzen 7 3700X, WSL2). docs/benchmarks.md has the versions and the commands to run it again.
gawain reads Python with ruff_python_parser and checks types with ty, both by Astral , or with pyrefly , by Meta.
I don't know, I just like the Arthurian tales. Gawain is a knight of the Round Table, and the mascot is the Green Knight's axe with the green girdle from Sir Gawain and the Green Knight .

Finishing negotiations for disputed South China Sea agreement will be a ‘tall order’, analysts say, amid China-Philippines tensions.
A long-awaited pact between the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and China for a “code of conduct” in the disputed South China Sea is unlikely to materialise during the regional bloc’s annual gathering of leaders in Manila this week, analysts and officials say.
The agreement would aim to manage tensions and prevent conflict at sea. But talks have dragged on for more than 20 years. In 2023, foreign ministers agreed to work towards finalising the accord within three years.
That deadline fell on 2026 – the year the Philippines took its turn as chair of ASEAN. Under its leadership, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) said negotiators have met at least once a month.
But they have fallen short of arriving at a consensus ahead of the summit.
“I just want to say that at this point in time, 80 percent of the document itself is finished,” DFA Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro said on Saturday, adding that there are some ‘salient’ points that still need to be ironed out.
She has previously said that geographical scope is one of the contentious issues. Beijing insists it has jurisdiction over nearly the entire South China Sea despite a 2016 international ruling invalidating that claim.
The Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia, Brunei and Indonesia also have overlapping territorial claims.
The Philippines would also like the accord to respect the rights of countries outside the region, according to DFA spokesman Dominic Xavier Imperial. Half of the world’s merchant ships pass through the South China Sea.
But the country may be caught between a rock and a hard place.
“You can’t win it because if you get a good document, you’ll be accused of railroading or it would come across as self-serving. But if it’s a bad document, the Marcos Jr administration will be seen as a weak government,” Aries Arugay, a political scientist at the University of the Philippines, said.
China has consistently accused the United States and its allies, who regularly conduct freedom of navigation operations with the Philippines, of interference.
Tensions between Manila and Beijing have escalated since Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr took office in 2022. The China Coast Guard has repeatedly deployed water cannon against Philippine vessels and maritime confrontations have resulted in collisions and, on one occasion, a Filipino soldier losing a finger.
In recent weeks, the two countries have been engaged in a war of words.
In September, Philippine Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro’s public response to a handwritten note rejecting the 2016 South China Sea ruling – reportedly from Beijing’s military attache in Seoul – went viral.
“Perhaps basic decency and behaviour is what China needs to do,” Teodoro, who has been barred from entering China, said.
A month later, Beijing’s ambassador to Manila, Jing Quan, told reporters that if China wanted to use force, “we may easily win. But no, we will not choose force. We love peace”. The statement was made in response to a question about Teodoro calling China a “troublemaker”, but which Marcos said “sounded like a threat”.
What followed was a barrage of social media posts by Philippine officials criticising Jing, with the Chinese embassy replying in kind. Senators called for the expulsion of the Chinese envoy.
And, in late October, China accused Teodoro of a late invitation to the ASEAN defence ministers’ meeting in Cebu. Without ample time to prepare, it said it could only send its Manila-based defence attache.
“When that happened, I think the concern, especially on the part of the DFA, was, ‘We don’t want China not sending their premier. It would not look good on us as a host country,’” Lucio Pitlo, past president of the Philippine Association for Chinese Studies, said.
With just days before world leaders were due to arrive in Manila, diplomats from both sides stepped in.
In a phone call, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi told Lazaro, his Philippine counterpart, to rein in politicians.
“The Philippines should strengthen restraint over the relevant individuals and send a rational and unified voice on its policy toward China,” Wang said in a statement released by the Chinese embassy in Manila.
Lazaro described the conversation as having been “frank and constructive”.
However, the DFA followed up with a statement saying it found public commentary by certain government officials “regrettable”.
“Whatever personal convictions public officials may hold, their public platforms carry institutional responsibilities,” it said. “They may not pursue preferred approaches toward China, or any other international partner, without regard for the consequences on the government’s overall policy.”
Some analysts say the spat has further exposed division within the Marcos administration.
“They’re airing dirty laundry out there. It doesn’t communicate coherence. It doesn’t project a unified stance. This could have been an internal memo,” Arugay said.
But Pitlo said the last-ditch diplomatic effort had achieved its objective. Chinese Premier Li Qiang is now attending the ASEAN Leaders’ Summit in Manila.
Despite this, Pitlo shares pessimism about leaders reaching a conclusion to negotiations for a code of conduct in the South China Sea.
“I think with all the concerns about trade protectionism, the disruption in supply chains, economic issues will be very high in the agenda. I think it will be a tall order to get the code of conduct done.”

US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
The US has not confirmed the Ukrainian president's comments. A US official told the BBC "many ideas continue to be discussed but any final deal will have to be agreed to by both parties".
Zelensky's remarks came after US envoys met him and Russian President Vladimir Putin as part of US efforts to end the war between their two countries.
Kyiv has long sought membership of the military alliance, but this has previously been opposed by the US and others, while Russia has said another Nato member on its border was unacceptable.
Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and currently controls most of the industrial Donbas region. Zelensky has consistently said Ukraine was unwilling to give up sovereign territory.
"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelensky said in remarks released by his office on Saturday.
He went on to say that if he received a specific proposal that contained security guarantees, no constraints on Ukraine's military and funds to rebuild the country, he would put it to a referendum.
US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to the Irish capital, Dublin, on Thursday to meet Zelensky, after a round of talks with Putin in Moscow.
Comments by both Putin and Kremlin officials suggest that Russia's position on the war has not shifted. It has previously proposed limits on the size of Ukraine's military, territorial concessions and Kyiv's guaranteed neutrality as conditions of a peace deal.
Ukraine has rejected these suggestions, arguing that such constraints would hamper its ability to stave off any future invasion.
Other Nato members apart from the US are wary of membership for Ukraine - and it is understood that Ukraine itself sees it as unrealistic.
The Kremlin has always been fiercely opposed, too. It is one reason why Russia started this war in the first place.
It is possible the US envoys were exploring Ukraine's "red lines" when it comes to occupied land in the Donbas. Zelensky recently said that the two American mediators believed Kyiv only had to cede territory to achieve peace and were applying pressure, keen to do a deal as soon as possible.
Ukraine is sure that Russia's ambitions are far greater and has long seen Nato as its only sure protection.
So it is also possible that Zelensky made this suggestion public to re-open a discussion that had been considered all but closed.
He said the idea was now "back on the agenda" as part of an "extremely difficult conversation" on European security in his latest remarks.
It also looks like Ukrainian push-back against Russia's renewed hardline stance. Moscow now talks about a "new European security architecture", which is long-standing Russian code for a weaker Nato.
The issue appears to have been the main focus at the latest round of talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi this week.
Hours after Zelensky's remarks, Jared Kushner appeared keen to dampen down any US offer of Nato membership for Ukraine, urging "confidentiality" in a sensitive process.
He said that "maximalist" proposals had been reported from the negotiations, along with "strong political rhetoric".
In what read like a reproach to Kyiv, Kushner referred to "private discussions" aimed at exploring new ideas about ending what he called a "horrible war".
He said the hope was that those ideas might lead to new proposals or breakthroughs.
Russia currently occupies roughly a fifth of Ukrainian territory, including most of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions that compose the Donbas.
It has insisted again that it will not agree to a ceasefire until a final peace deal is in place that would include Ukraine ceding control of those parts of the Donbas Russian troops have not captured, in addition to the Crimean peninsula Moscow annexed illegally in 2014.
The latest round of talks come after a period of fraught relations between Kyiv and Washington over Ukrainian strikes on oil facilities deep inside Russia, which US President Donald Trump had asked Ukraine to pause to facilitate the supply of Russian diesel to ease global fuel prices.
Zelensky then accused US officials of limiting Ukraine's Starlink internet service , which it uses to co-ordinate defensive operations, while Trump said it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president" and called for fresh elections.
Elections are suspended while Ukraine remains under martial law, but Zelensky has previously said he was willing to hold them within months of a peace deal being reached and would give up the presidency in exchange for Nato membership.
Rosenberg: Uncompromising Putin ups demands for peace with Ukraine
US envoys meet Zelensky in Dublin after talks with Putin in Moscow
